In terms of Section 70(1) of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act, 
No. 16 of 2023, the Central Bank 
is required to prepare and publish the Financial Stability Review (FSR) on or before the thirty-first 
day in the month of October of each year.
 
 Fulfilling this obligation, FSR of 2026 encapsulates the 
developments in the financial system, the risks and vulnerabilities identified thereof, and the policy

measures taken by the Central Bank and other regulatory institutions in addressing such risks during 
the review period, which primarily covers data up to end June 2026. However, more updated selected 
developments are also reported in the publication. Data may include calculations made specially for 
this publication based on information obtained from various sources.

FINANCIAL STABILITY REVIEW 2026
XX

Sri Lanka's macrofinancial environment remained stable, supporting financial stability during H1 of 2026 while external 
headwinds intensified.  Global macrofinancial conditions became more challenging, exerting negative spillovers on 
the domestic economy. Heightened geopolitical tensions, including the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, 
elevated global uncertainty, renewed inflationary pressures, tightened global financial conditions, increasing trade

fragmentation, policy uncertainty, climate related risks such as the El Niño phenomenon and elevated volatility in 
financial markets created a challenging external environment, with potential implications for domestic macroeconomic 
and financial stability. Rising energy and commodity prices, disruptions to key trade routes, and heightened uncertainty 
contributed to a resurgence of inflationary pressures and increased downside risks to the global outlook. These

developments heightened the exposure of emerging markets and developing economies including Sri Lanka to 
adverse spillovers through trade, capital flow, financing, and exchange rate channels, as well as climate related 
shocks.
Against this backdrop, domestic macrofinancial conditions remained broadly conducive to financial stability, underpinned 
by continued economic growth, improved fiscal performance and conducive financial sector developments. However,

the rapid expansion of credit and emerging pressure from global macrofinancial conditions warranted close monitoring 
of the financial system. Credit to the private sector expanded significantly amid the recovery in economic activity and 
relatively accommodative monetary conditions that prevailed during much of the review period, with particularly strong 
expansions observed in household lending, vehicle financing, and gold backed lending. Consequently, financial

intermediation strengthened, as credit growth continued to outpace deposit growth. Moreover, the private sector credit 
cycle remained in an expansionary phase, with the widening private sector credit gap indicating the potential buildup 
of systemic vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, renewed inflationary pressures, stemming mainly from higher global energy 
and commodity prices and strengthening domestic demand, along with significant growth in credit to the private

sector prompted a tightening of domestic monetary policy in May 2026. Consequently, this contributed towards further 
upward adjustments in market interest rates and Government securities yields. In addition, macroprudential measures 
in the form of Loan to Value (LTV)  limits on vehicle and gold backed lending, were introduced amid significant credit 
growth to mitigate the buildup of systemic risks within the financial sector.

Fiscal performance strengthened further, reducing reliance on domestic financing and supporting the reallocation of 
financial sector resources towards private sector activities. Nevertheless, the external sector remained vulnerable to 
adverse global developments, particularly through commodity prices, with potential spillovers through trade, tourism,

workers’ remittances, and exchange rate channels. At the same time, growing interconnectedness among financial 
institutions, increasing digitalisation of financial services and rapid developments in financial technologies, together 
with rising cyber security threats, have emerged as important considerations for financial sector resilience. Further, 
the increasing frequency and severity of climate related events added to the macrofinancial risk landscape, posing 
challenges to stability.

challenges to stability. 
Looking ahead, Sri Lanka's macrofinancial outlook remains broadly stable despite potential headwinds on several 
fronts. Continued economic growth, stronger fiscal performance, and improved financial sector resilience would 
provide important safeguards against potential shocks. Nevertheless, heightened geopolitical tensions, renewed 
inflationary pressures, tighter global financial conditions, climate related risks, and rapid credit expansion could pose

challenges to financial stability going forward. Accordingly, preserving macroeconomic stability, maintaining adequate 
capital and liquidity buffers, strengthening risk management practices and ensuring that credit expansion remains 
consistent with underlying economic fundamentals will be important for safeguarding the stability of the financial 
system. Thus, the Central Bank will continue to closely monitor and assess emerging risks and vulnerabilities to the

financial system and take proactive and timely macroprudential measures, where necessary.

Stress in domestic financial markets, as measured by the Financial Stress Index (FSI)1, remained subdued during the 
first eight months of 2026, despite a temporary increase in March 2026 amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty. The 
FSI remained contained at low level, as relatively stable conditions in the Government securities market and money 
market offset intermittent increases in stock and domestic foreign exchange market stress.

market offset intermittent increases in stock and domestic foreign exchange market stress.
Stock market performance moderated during the first eight months of 2026, amid heightened geopolitical tensions, 
global financial market uncertainty, rising energy prices, the domestic inflation outlook and tighter monetary conditions. 
Stock price indices remained subdued, while market liquidity moderated and volatility increased. Market valuation

indicators increased modestly but remained broadly in line with their long term averages and below those of most 
regional peers. Persistent net foreign outflows underscored the importance of attracting stable, long term capital 
inflows to strengthen market liquidity and resilience.
Conditions in the Government securities market tightened, with yields increasing across maturities. Evolving market

expectations, geopolitical uncertainty and tighter monetary conditions were reflected in the upward adjustment in 
yields. Despite strong fiscal performance and robust demand for Government securities, secondary market liquidity 
remained constrained, with trading concentrated within a limited range of maturities. Foreign investment recorded a 
modest recovery towards the latter part of the review period as yields adjusted upwards and exchange rate conditions

improved, although overall foreign participation remained low.
The domestic foreign exchange market experienced some pressure, with conditions improving in the latter part of 
review period. Heightened geopolitical tensions, rising energy prices, increased import demand and changing investor 
sentiment caused to the depreciation of the Sri Lanka rupee against the US dollar and several other major currencies.

Nevertheless, conditions subsequently improved, supported by policy measures and continued foreign exchange 
inflows from workers’ remittances, export proceeds and tourism earnings, while exchange rate volatility moderated 
and interbank transaction volumes exhibited a gradual recovery.
Domestic money market activity strengthened further, with increased repo and call money market transactions. State-

owned banks remained key net lenders, while domestic private banks continued to be net borrowers, reflecting the 
asymmetric distribution of liquidity. The Average Weighted Call Money Rate (AWCMR) and Average Weighted Repo 
Rate (AWRR) exhibited some intermittent upward pressure during the review period and subsequently returned to 
broad alignment with the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR), while overall money market liquidity remained in surplus.

Payment and settlement infrastructure remained operationally resilient during the review period, while continued 
growth in digital payments and measures to strengthen settlement risk management, interoperability and accessibility 
supported payment system resilience. Nevertheless, the increasing reliance on digital channels continued to warrant 
close monitoring of cyber, operational and third-party risks.

close monitoring of cyber, operational and third-party risks.
Overall, domestic financial markets and payment infrastructures remained resilient during the review period despite 
heightened global uncertainty, tighter domestic monetary conditions and moderate pressure on foreign exchange 
and stock markets. Maintaining macroeconomic stability, strengthening investor confidence, broadening foreign

investment base and deepening domestic financial markets and payment infrastructures would enhance resilience 
against external and domestic shocks.

the year.
Confidence in the Financial System
Respondents’ overall confidence 4 in the financial system, 
as measured by the net percentage balance, declined in H1 
of 2026 before re cording a slight improvement in H2 2026. 
Overall, short term confidence remained lower in 2026 
compared to 2025, although it remained in positive territory.

compared to 2025, although it remained in positive territory. 
Medium term confidence exhibited a broadly similar pattern 
across the two survey rounds. A substantial proportion 
of respondents e xpressed a ‘Fairly Confident’ outlook, 
indicating that confidence in financial system stability 
remained moderate.

Event

of a high impact negative event occurring within the financial

of a high impact negative event occurring within the financial

probability of such an event materialising in the short term 
increased, as reflected by the net percentage balance, 5 
reversing the declining trend observed in previous years. In 
contrast, the perceived probability of a high impact negative 
event occurring in the medium term moderated slightly in 
H2 of 2026, following a marginal increase in H1 of 2026 ,

H2 of 2026, following a marginal increase in H1 of 2026 ,

term risks.

and associated spillovers.  This was followed by ‘ General

impact of ‘Risks Related to Financial Infrastructure’ increased 
slightly in H2 of 2026 compared to H1 of 2026 indicating a

other risk categories declined.

Financial institution s remained resilient durin g the twelve month period that ended in June 2026, supported by 
continued recovery in economic activity, increased earnings, and adequate capital buffers, despite the adverse 
impacts from natural disasters and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Financial intermediation improved across the 
banking and finance companies (FCs) sectors, supporting the overall economic recovery during the period. Credit

demand was particularly high for certain sectors, including vehicle and gold backed facilities. However, elevated credit 
expansion contributed to some moderation in liquidity and capital positions, although the sectors continued to maintain 
adequate buffers above the respective regulatory minimum requirements. Nevertheless, rapid and concentrated 
credit growth, increases in Stage 2 loans, cross-border lending, and interconnectedness between banks and FCs

arising from excessive lending to FCs warrant close monitoring. Considering the potential build-up of systemic risks 
from excessive credit growth, the Central Bank introduced several macroprudential policy measures, including 
tightened loan-to-value (LTV) limits for vehicle loans and introduced LTV limits and higher risk weights for gold backed  
facilities.1 These measures, together with the policy rate adjustment in May 2026 and the extension of the temporary

surcharge on motor vehicle imports, are expected to moderate credit growth over the coming quarters.
The Banking Soundness Index, an indicator to assess the overall soundness of the banking sector, declined marginally 
during the first half of 2026. The banking sector credit expanded significantly amid robust private sector demand, with 
notable growth in consumption, trade, financial services, construction, and offshore lending. Asset quality indicators

continued to improve, supported by the expansion of the credit base and a reduction in outstanding Stage 3 loans, 
while the improvement in the Stage 3 impairment coverage ratio provided an additional cushion against unexpected 
credit losses. However, increasing Stage 2 loans during Q2 of 2026 highlights the potential risk of future downward 
migration of loans. The sector’s exposure to the Government and state owned enterprises declined amid strong

private sector credit demand during the period, although it remained sizeable. Liquidity coverage ratios and net stable 
funding ratio remained well above the regulatory minimums, though moderated slightly as banks reallocated liquid 
assets towards lending. Capital ratios also declined, as risk weighted assets expanded faster than capital due to 
strong credit expansion, narrowing the sector’s capacity to absorb unexpected losses.

strong credit expansion, narrowing the sector’s capacity to absorb unexpected losses.
The FCs sector also demonstrated robust growth during the period, with lending accelerating sharply amid increased 
demand for motor vehicle financing, following the relaxation of vehicle import restrictions, and the continued expansion 
of gold backed lending, supported by the elevated gold prices. The concentration of credit in vehicle and gold backed

lending increased the sector’s vulnerability to adverse movements in the underlying collateral values. To contain 
these risks, the Central Bank proactively introduced several macroprudential policy measures. Asset quality indicators 
improved, supported by the significant expansion of the credit portfolio and a reduction in outstanding Stage 3 loans. 
However, increase in Stage 2 exposures and the moderation in impairment coverage warranted continued vigilance on

asset quality. The sector’s liquidity buffers declined amid the rapid balance sheet expansion. Meanwhile, borrowings 
remained elevated at end June 2026, underpinned by the sector’s growing reliance on funding from banks. The 
aggregate capital ratio of the sector remained well above the regulatory requirements, despite a decline in capital 
buffers resulting from the growth in lending.

buffers resulting from the growth in lending.
The insurance sector continued to expand with an improvement in insurance penetration during the period, supported 
by strong growth in gross written premiums and assets. Profitability in both the long term and general insurance 
subsectors moderated, although their capital adequacy ratios remained well above the respective regulatory minimum

requirements. Cyclone Ditwah generated substantial insurance claims, and the settlement of these claims could exert 
certain pressure on the underwriting performance, liquidity, and capital positions of general insurers.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being adopted across the 
global financial services industry at a pace that has drawn 
sustained supervisory attention. AI is elevating cyber risk 
from an operational concern to a core financial stability 
issue, principally through the scale effects it unleashes 
across shared technologies. 1 Against this background, 
the Central Bank surveyed all Licensed Banks (LBs) in 
Sri Lanka in November 2025 on AI adoption, governance,

Sri Lanka in November 2025 on AI adoption, governance, 
risk management, data readiness and strategic priorities. 2 
However, as AI is rapidly evolving, current status could be 
slightly different. This Special Note summarizes the key 
findings3 and examines the emerging risks with potential 
systemic implications with particular emphasis on cyber 
security resilience of LBs.
Current State of AI Adoption in LBs
In total, 69% of LBs have commenced some form of AI

Current State of AI Adoption in LBs
In total, 69% of LBs have commenced some form of AI 
activity, although the depth of adoption remains shallow. No 
AI usage and no immediate plans were reported by 31% of 
LBs, while 21% were at exploratory or feasibility stage and 
17% had pilot projects under development. Further, 31% 
have moved to live deployment, 10% in limited areas, 17% 
across multiple functions and 4% with extensive integration. 
No bank reported an AI-first operational model.

No bank reported an AI-first operational model.
Prevailing use cases cluster around fraud and anti-money 
laundering monitoring, credit scoring, customer facing 
chatbots, document processing and internal productivity 
applications. Faster service delivery, round-the-clock 
availability and lower service costs were identified as the 
principal customer benefits, while clear disclosure of AI 
usage was the most cited trust building measure. Generative

usage was the most cited trust building measure. Generative 
AI applications are emerging in customer service and internal 
knowledge management.
Governance and Risk Management Practices
AI governance structures are still in the early stages of 
forming. 23% of LBs manage AI through integration with 
existing risk committees and an equal share through cross 
functional working groups, while 8% have established a board 
level AI oversight committee and 15% a senior management

level AI oversight committee and 15% a senior management 
AI steering committee. AI governance arrangements are yet 
to be formed in 17% of LBs.
Risk assessment practices display a comparable skew. 
Banks concentrate on technology, operational, compliance 
and model risk, while credit, market and liquidity risk receive 
less attention. AI is presently treated as a technological 
deployment matter rather than a driver of financial risk.

Third Party Dependence and Concentration
62% of LBs reported partnerships with a small group of 
international technology companies. Engagement with local 
technology firms (24%), regional fintech companies and 
open source solutions (21% each) and system integrators 
and AI consultancies (17% each) is substantially lower.
Due diligence on AI service providers and data security 
requirements in contracts stand at 17%, service level

requirements in contracts stand at 17%, service level 
agreements at 16%, exit strategies and data portability 
clauses at 14%, board approval for AI outsourcing and 
vendor business continuity arrangements at 13%, and the 
right to audit vendor operations at only 10%. Narrow provider 
concentration combined with contractual controls that need 
strengthening is the most consequential finding of the survey.

most cited adoption challenges (15% of responses), alongside

The principal systemic risk arises not from novel attack 
techniques but from the speed, frequency and breadth with 
which AI allows vulnerabilities to be discovered and exploited 
across widely used technologies. Industry data indicate that 
activity by AI enabled adversaries rose by 89% between 
2024 and 2025, while the average time taken by attackers 
to move laterally within a compromised network fell by 65%

to move laterally within a compromised network fell by 65% 
to 29 minutes.4 The window for detection and containment is 
narrowing towards machine speed.
These dynamics bear directly on LBs. AI lowers the cost and 
raises the impact of attacks on banks and their customers. 
Generative models enable phishing and business email 
compromise in fluent Sinhala, Tamil and English at scale, 
while synthetic voice and video permit impersonation 
of customers and senior officers, threatening remote

of customers and senior officers, threatening remote 
onboarding, video based customer identification and 
payment authorization controls. In this context, an emerging 
risk can be observed in relation to fraud typologies in 
domestic retail payment channels.
Adoption also expands the attack surface. Model endpoints, 
application programming interfaces, training data 
repositories and vector databases sit outside conventional 
perimeter controls, and attack vectors specific to AI systems,

perimeter controls, and attack vectors specific to AI systems, 
such as prompt injections, training data poisoning and model 
inversion are not addressed by existing control baselines. 
Unsanctioned staff use of public generative AI tools creates 
a further channel for confidential data to leave the bank's 
control boundary.
Most consequentially for financial stability, AI concentrates 
exposure. Where banks rely on the same limited set of

exposure. Where banks rely on the same limited set of 
cloud and model providers, a compromise or outage at a 
single provider ceases to be idiosyncratic and becomes a 
common mode failure across institutions. Emerging markets 
and developing economies are disproportionately exposed, 
sharing the same global digital infrastructure as advanced 
economies, but with fewer defensive resources, more 
limited supervisory capacity and greater reliance on smaller

limited supervisory capacity and greater reliance on smaller 
vendors whose patching cycles are longer, extending the 
window during which known vulnerabilities remain open. For 
Sri Lanka, this is the operative warning.
Offsetting these exposures, AI strengthens defensive 
capability through anomaly detection, behavioral analytics 
and automated triage. The supervisory expectation is 
therefore symmetrical that banks investing in AI for revenue

therefore symmetrical that banks investing in AI for revenue 
generating functions are expected to invest commensurately 
in machine speed defense. Prevention alone is no longer 
sufficient. Segmentation, zero trust architecture, disciplined 
access control and secure by design practices that limit the 
blast radius of a breach and constrain lateral movement are 
now central to resilience.

The Household and Corporate sectors 1 play a central role in the financial system through their close linkages with 
financial institutions and their contribution to economic activity. Households support consumption and savings, while 
corporates drive production, investment and employment. As major borrowers from the financial system, their financial 
positions and capacity to service debt directly influence the asset quality and profitability of financial institutions.

Adverse developments in household income and corporate earnings can increase credit losses and constrain lending, 
with broader implications for economic activity. Accordingly, assessing vulnerabilities in these sectors is important for 
the early identification of risks to financial system stability.
Credit extended to the Household 2 and Institutional 3 sectors continued to expand strongly during H1 of 2026,

reflecting robust credit demand supported by improving economic activity. Household sector credit growth remained 
elevated, although the pace of expansion moderated slightly during Q2 of 2026 following a sustained acceleration 
over the previous two years. Institutional sector credit also recorded robust growth, supported primarily by bank 
lending. Although the expansion in credit strengthens financial intermediation, it underscores the need for continued

monitoring of the pace, composition and quality of credit. Meanwhile, the risk profile of Household sector borrowers 
improved further in H1 of 2026, with the majority of borrowers remaining within lower risk categories. Institutional 
sector borrowers also exhibited a broadly sound credit risk profile, with exposures remaining largely concentrated 
in lower risk categories. Nevertheless, borrower risk profiles in the Non-Bank Financial Institution (NBFI) sector

continued to be relatively weaker compared to the banking sector, warranting continued monitoring from a financial 
stability perspective. Looking ahead, tighter monetary conditions and the recently introduced Loan to Value (LTV) 4 
measures are expected to moderate credit growth gradually, particularly in the Household sector. Nonetheless, recent 
improvements recorded in repayment performance and borrower credit quality may provide some support to the 
resilience of both sectors.

resilience of both sectors.
Listed Non-Financial Corporates (NFCs), recorded stronger business activity during H1 of 2026, supported by broad 
based revenue growth across most sectors. The improvement in revenue was driven mainly by the Automobile, Power 
and Energy, and Manufacturing sectors, reflecting favourable sector specific developments and improved business 
conditions. Despite the increase in revenue, overall net profit recorded a decline during H1 of 2026 compared to

previous year. However, underlying profitability conditions among NFCs showed signs of improvement, as reflected 
in increased median net profit and profit growth among a majority of firms. The decline in overall profitability has been 
driven primarily by few corporates. Consequently, key profitability indicators weakened, and the overall debt servicing 
capacity of listed NFCs moderated, with the aggregate Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR) declining during the period.

However, leverage conditions improved modestly and the aggregate ICR remained comfortably above one, indicating 
that listed NFCs continued to generate sufficient profits to meet their interest obligations on average. Overall, the 
listed NFC sector remained resilient despite mixed profitability trends. Most firms maintained healthy debt servicing 
capacity, limiting overall credit risk to the financial institutions.

Chapter 5
Policies for Financial
Stability
The Central Bank deployed macroprudential tools along with other prudential measures during the period under review 
against the backdrop of rapid credit expansion in the economy in its capacity as the designated macroprudential 
authority under the Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act, No. 16 of 2023. The increasing exposures of Licensed Banks 
(LBs) and Finance Companies (FCs) towards motor vehicle related credit and gold backed lending coupled with price

volatility of underlying collaterals warranted strengthening of borrower based macroprudential policies. In response, 
the Central Bank issued forward guidance in March 2026 on managing risk in gold backed lending to LBs and FCs, 
with a view of promoting greater prudence in such lending activities. Subsequently, in response to the continued rapid 
growth in motor vehicle related lending and gold backed lending, the Central Bank implemented macroprudential

measures aimed at containing excessive leverage, enhancing borrower resilience, and mitigating systemic risks. 
Accordingly, the Central Bank introduced a Loan to Value (LTV) limit of 70% for credit facilities backed by gold collateral 
during May 2026. Further, the Central Bank reduced the maximum permissible LTV ratio for motor vehicle related 
credit in November 2025 and May 2026. These revisions not only reinforced prudential safeguards but also simplified

the LTV framework applicable for motor vehicles related credit facilities, enhancing its operational effectiveness.
In addition to macroprudential policies, the Central Bank introduced several prudential regulations and policy 
measures to strengthen the overall financial system stability. Accordingly, in conjunction with broader macroprudential 
tightening measures, the Central Bank tightened the risk weights applicable to gold backed lending by LBs and

FCs, including the removal of the zero risk weights previously applicable for certain gold backed credit facilities 
for the purpose of determining Capital Adequacy Requirements. The Central Bank introduced the Framework for 
Banking Sector Consolidation to promote a stronger, more resilient, and sustainable banking sector through the 
consolidation of small sized banks.  Further, the regulatory framework for FCs sector was further enhanced through

the introduction of several directions while extending the continued supervisory efforts to strengthen compliance of 
FCs sector with Anti Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing  
(AML/CFT/CPF) requirements. Moreover, various regulatory initiatives were implemented during the period under 
consideration to strengthen risk management, enhance institutional resilience, operational soundness, and smooth

functioning of the LBs and FCs sectors.
Moreover, the Central Bank continued to strengthen the resilience, efficiency, and inclusiveness of the financial 
system through a range of policy, supervisory, and consumer-focused initiatives. The Central Bank took further policy 
initiatives to safeguard consumers by strengthening the security of digital payment methods and enhancing public

awareness of scam related risks. As part of the Central Bank’s efforts to strengthen the resolution regime of the 
country, the resolution plans are being progressively developed for Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) to support 
the effective management of institutional distress. The Central Bank continued to strengthen the financial consumer 
protection framework via enhanced market conduct supervision, regulatory oversight, complaint management, and

financial consumer awareness initiatives. The financial literacy and public awareness of sound financial management 
practices continued to be promoted as part of the Central Bank’s efforts to advance financial inclusion. Moreover, the 
Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) of the Central Bank continued to strengthen Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT/CPF framework 
through a range of regulatory, supervisory, and policy initiatives during the period under review.

through a range of regulatory, supervisory, and policy initiatives during the period under review.
Amid heightened global uncertainties, evolving geopolitical and macrofinancial risks and the build-up of vulnerabilities 
within the domestic financial system, the Central Bank remains committed to safeguarding the stability and resilience 
of the financial system. Accordingly, the Central Bank will continue to closely monitor market developments, global

and domestic macroeconomic and financial conditions, and calibrate its macroprudential stance and implement 
appropriate prudential policy actions, to mitigate emerging vulnerabilities and preserve financial system stability.

Summary
The Sri Lankan economy continued to record robust growth in 2025, demonstrating 
increased resilience to both domestic and global shocks. The year was characterised by 
elevated global uncertainties, particularly related to trade policies, as well as the impact 
of an extreme weather event towards the end of the year. Despite these challenges, the 
economy grew by 5% in real terms in 2025, marking the second consecutive year of

economy grew by 5% in real terms in 2025, marking the second consecutive year of 
expansion, supported by post-crisis macroeconomic stabilisation measures and ongoing 
economic reforms. A drop in the unemployment rate was also observed during the year. 
Inflation, which had been negative for eleven consecutive months, turned positive in 
August 2025 and accelerated gradually thereafter, supported by the easing of deflationary

August 2025 and accelerated gradually thereafter, supported by the easing of deflationary 
pressures in the energy and transport sectors, alongside rising food inflation. Core inflation 
stayed at lower positive levels in 2025, indicating that demand conditions are still subdued. 
Supported by benign inflation and anchored inflation expectations, the Central Bank 
further eased its accommodative monetary policy stance, leading to continued downward

further eased its accommodative monetary policy stance, leading to continued downward 
adjustments in interest rates and facilitating greater consumption and investment. As a 
result, lending to the private sector saw a record high and broad-based expansion during 
the year. This growth was further driven by increased demand for vehicle imports after 
the complete removal of import restrictions in early 2025. External sector performance

the complete removal of import restrictions in early 2025. External sector performance 
improved further in 2025, as reflected by the current account, which recorded a surplus for 
the third consecutive year. Despite the widened trade deficit, the current account recorded 
a higher surplus in 2025 than in the previous two years, supported by a stronger services 
account surplus, a substantial improvement in workers’ remittances, and a narrowing of

account surplus, a substantial improvement in workers’ remittances, and a narrowing of 
the primary income account deficit. Improved foreign exchange inflows enhanced liquidity 
in the domestic foreign exchange market, thus enabling the Central Bank to purchase 
foreign exchange and build external reserves to around USD 6.8 bn by end 2025, despite 
the highest external debt service payments since 2020. The Sri Lanka rupee experienced

the highest external debt service payments since 2020. The Sri Lanka rupee experienced 
some depreciation during the year after two years of appreciation, mainly due to higher 
merchandise imports, especially in the second half of the year. Such exchange rate 
movements were consistent with the evolving external conditions under a flexible regime.

Conclusion
Following the earlier inflation surge, the economy 
experienced a deflationary episode driven mainly 
by significant reductions in energy and transport 
prices, supported by favourable weather conditions, 
lower global energy prices, and statistical base 
effects. As inflation returned to positive territory 
in late 2025, the pace of increase remained 
moderate, indicating a gradual and orderly 
normalisation of price dynamics. Economic growth

moderate, indicating a gradual and orderly 
normalisation of price dynamics. Economic growth 
and core inflation dynamics suggest that underlying 
demand conditions did not weaken significantly 
during the deflationary period episode. Moreover, 
other macroeconomic indicators also suggest that 
economic activity continued to increase, rather 
than recording a persistent slowdown. Taken 
together, these developments suggest that the 
recent persistence in inflation largely reflects the

recent persistence in inflation largely reflects the 
gradual normalisation of price dynamics amid a 
high cost base, rather than a sustained contraction 
in demand. While the recent deflationary episode 
and persistently low inflation may suggest scope for 
a lower inflation target, such considerations need 
to be viewed in the context of Sri Lanka’s structural 
characteristics. As a small, open economy that is 
more susceptible to supply-side shocks, including

more susceptible to supply-side shocks, including 
weather-related disruptions and external shocks,  
Sri Lanka requires a relatively higher inflation target 
and a wider deviation margin compared to larger 
and more advanced economies to accommodate 
such fluctuations and ensure effective policy 
implementation.

BOX 02
Addressing Data Gaps in Private Sector Wage Dynamics Using EPF Based Formal Sector Wage Rate Index 
Rationale for Using Superannuation 
Contribution Data
Given the limitations of existing wage statistics and 
the need for a timely indicator to assess private 
sector wage dynamics, administrative data sources 
were considered. Among these, superannuation 
contribution records were identified as a suitable 
basis for developing a high-frequency private

contribution records were identified as a suitable 
basis for developing a high-frequency private 
sector wage rate index to enhance the monitoring 
of labour cost developments relevant for 
macroeconomic and monetary policy analysis. The 
analysis is based on aggregated EPF administrative 
data, and no individual level information is used, 
ensuring confidentiality of contributors.

Data Source and Methodological Approach
The wage rate index is constructed using 
administrative data obtained from the EPF, 
covering the period from January 2017 to 
December 2025. The dataset comprises  
employer-reported contribution records submitted 
through manual, online, and e-media platforms, 
with online and e-media channels accounting 
for many contribution values, ensuring broad 
coverage of formal sector employment. It includes 
key variables such as employer identifiers, number

key variables such as employer identifiers, number 
of employees, contribution values, and reporting 
periods, enabling the compilation of a  
high-frequency wage indicator. Given differences 
in reporting lags, more timely partial datasets 
can be utilised for policy analysis, while finalised 
datasets are used for official publication.
The index is compiled using January 2017 as 
the base period, reflecting relatively stable wage 
conditions. Among alternative index number

the base period, reflecting relatively stable wage 
conditions. Among alternative index number 
approaches evaluated, the Laspeyres method was 
selected based on its empirical performance and 
consistency. This approach, which uses fixed  
base-period weights, is widely adopted in 
international practice and provides a stable 
measure of wage movements over time.

this index has several limitations. This index, which 
was introduced with December 1978 as the base

was introduced with December 1978 as the base

using statutory minimum wages rather than 
actual earnings. Minimum wages are not revised 
frequently, whereas total earnings comprising basic 
wages, variable payments, and various allowances 
may adjust more regularly in response to labour 
market conditions, limiting the index’s ability to 
capture the true dynamics of wage adjustments. In

capture the true dynamics of wage adjustments. In

development of an alternative private sector wage 
rate index using data from contributions to the

of constructing a more representative indicator of 
wage movements in the private sector.2

Conceptual Framework of the New Wage Rate 
Index
The wage rate index is designed to measure changes 
in formal sector wages over time rather than absolute 
wage levels. By focusing on relative movements, the 
index provides an indicator of wage growth dynamics 
that can be assessed across periods and considered 
alongside other macroeconomic indicators, including 
inflation and output measures.
The resulting wage rate index provides a stable time

inflation and output measures.
The resulting wage rate index provides a stable time 
series suitable for macroeconomic analysis. The use 
of administrative data enhances comparability over 
time and reduces volatility associated with sampling 
variation. Wage adjustments tend to occur with a 
delay relative to price movements, reflecting  
wage-setting mechanisms and institutional 
arrangements. In this context, the availability of 
a high-frequency wage rate index improves the

arrangements. In this context, the availability of 
a high-frequency wage rate index improves the 
monitoring of labour cost pressures and complements 
existing wage indicators derived from survey data and 
institutional wage adjustments. 
Implications for Monetary Policy and Labour 
Market Analysis
The new index offers timely and robust insights into 
the interplay between private sector wage growth, 
inflationary pressures, and broader macroeconomic

inflationary pressures, and broader macroeconomic 
conditions. Analysis of the index shows that wage 
growth responds not only to underlying economic 
activity but also to changes in the price level. 
Figure B 2.4 indicates that the new wage index has 
been catching up with the increase in price indices. 
For example, the pronounced increase in average 
wages during 2022–2023 reflects the impact of 
elevated inflation, underscoring the potential for

wages during 2022–2023 reflects the impact of 
elevated inflation, underscoring the potential for 
second-round effects in wage-setting behaviour. 
By capturing these dynamics more accurately 
than traditional indicators, the new wage index 
enhances the CBSL’s capacity to anticipate and 
respond to emerging inflationary pressures.
High-frequency administrative data are particularly 
valuable for forward-looking policy. With online 
and e-media submissions accounting for roughly

valuable for forward-looking policy. With online 
and e-media submissions accounting for roughly 
80% of EPF contributions, the monthly aggregation 
of this information enables more responsive 
monitoring of labour cost developments. The 
new wage index complements existing indicators, 
including the long-standing Formal Private Sector 
Minimum Wage Rate Index, by providing a 
broader, more representative measure of formal 
private sector wages, covering over 800,000

broader, more representative measure of formal 
private sector wages, covering over 800,000 
employees. This expanded coverage allows 
policymakers to track structural labour market 
trends with greater precision, supporting  
evidence-based decisions on monetary policy and 
wage-related interventions.
Strengthening Wage Monitoring and Future 
Directions
The compilation of the index represents a major 
enhancement in Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic data

The compilation of the index represents a major 
enhancement in Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic data 
infrastructure. Leveraging over 6 mn individual 
observations received over a period of 9 years, analysed 
using big data analytics techniques, the index establishes 
a foundation for regular, high-frequency monitoring 
of private sector wages. Moving forward, priority will 
be given to institutionalising data sharing, ensuring 
seamless integration of monthly contributions for policy

seamless integration of monthly contributions for policy 
analysis while maintaining semi-annual updates for the 
full dataset.
Beyond aggregate wage tracking, the 
administrative dataset offers significant analytical 
potential. Planned refinements include the 
development of sectoral indices to provide 
industry-specific insights into wage dynamics. 
In the longer term, integrating supplementary 
administrative datasets could allow the 
construction of a multi-dimensional framework

administrative datasets could allow the 
construction of a multi-dimensional framework 
for wage analysis, improving transparency and 
equipping policymakers and researchers with a 
comprehensive tool to assess evolving labour 
market conditions. Collectively, these initiatives 
position the index not only as a critical instrument 
for monitoring wages and inflation but also as 
a cornerstone for strengthening evidence-based 
macroeconomic policy in Sri Lanka. Going

a cornerstone for strengthening evidence-based 
macroeconomic policy in Sri Lanka. Going 
forward, the Central Bank intends to disseminate 
EPF-based Formal Sector Wage Rate Index statistics 
through its annual and semiannual publications.

The increasing adoption of renewable energy, 
particularly solar and wind, is reshaping electricity 
markets globally. In Sri Lanka, although the 
transition towards such non-conventional renewable 
energy sources commenced nearly a decade 
ago, it has only gained significant momentum 
following the removal of energy subsidies through 
the Government’s efforts in moving towards

following the removal of energy subsidies through 
the Government’s efforts in moving towards 
a more cost-reflective pricing mechanism for 
utilities in 2022. This policy decision created 
financial incentives for both the private sector and 
households to invest in their own renewable energy 
sources, thereby fulfilling energy needs with  
low-cost options and supporting the growing 
demand for electricity. 
Accordingly, capacity expansions were seen in the

demand for electricity. 
Accordingly, capacity expansions were seen in the 
renewable sector, particularly in solar energy, driven 
by the rapid investments in rooftop solar panels 
which accounted for nearly 9.4% of total electricity 
generation1 in 2025. This growing adoption of 
rooftop solar panels has reduced the reliance on 
relatively costly thermal generation amidst rising 
electricity demand. 
However, this rapid expansion in solar power 
presents several challenges. Particularly, the

However, this rapid expansion in solar power 
presents several challenges. Particularly, the 
mismatch between daytime solar power generation 
and nighttime peak demand creates complications 
in grid management and grid stability. This 
shortcoming can be resolved to a greater extent 
through battery storage systems. Offering higher 
feed-in tariff for the battery installed solar systems 
which supply electricity to the grid at peak hours 
and gradual transition into Net Plus System2 and

and gradual transition into Net Plus System2 and 
Time of Use tariffs3 are several solutions to promote 
investments in battery storage. Exploration of novel 
business models such as aggregators or community 
energy cooperatives to procure rooftop solar energy 
could be useful in grid management amidst rapid 
expansion in small scale solar energy producers.

towards solar power generation, it is prudent to

make futuristic plans on safe disposal/recycling of 
solar panels as well as batteries at the end of their 
life span. 
Timely and coordinated actions remain essential 
for this transition to continue and fully harness the 
potential of solar energy. Further, advancing this 
transition and supporting the growth of renewable 
generation is essential in light of growing volatility in

Summary
By sustaining price and financial system stability, the Central Bank’s policies in 2025 supported 
a conducive environment for high and sustainable economic growth. The Central Bank’s 
monetary easing cycle that commenced in mid-2023 continued throughout 2025, with 
one downward adjustment to the Overnight Policy Rate in May. This stance was retained 
in view of domestic deflationary conditions, well-anchored inflation expectations, weakening

in view of domestic deflationary conditions, well-anchored inflation expectations, weakening 
global demand, and ongoing trade-related uncertainties. Money market liquidity remained 
in surplus during the year, largely supported by substantial net foreign exchange purchases 
by the Central Bank. With improved liquidity conditions, the Central Bank suspended  
liquidity-injecting Open Market Operations from end January 2025. The overall easing of

liquidity-injecting Open Market Operations from end January 2025. The overall easing of 
monetary conditions supported broad declines in interest rates and strong growth in private 
sector credit, while inflation returned to positive territory from August 2025. However, in the 
second half of 2025, a temporary uptick in short-term market interest rates was observed 
owing to uneven distribution of rupee liquidity among participatory institutions and increased

owing to uneven distribution of rupee liquidity among participatory institutions and increased 
government financing needs, particularly in the aftermath of Cyclone Ditwah. Despite this, the 
Central Bank refrained from injecting liquidity into the market, given the overall excess liquidity 
and continued growth of private sector credit. By early 2026, short term interest rates adjusted 
downwards as rupee liquidity became more evenly distributed. As the inflation rate remained

downwards as rupee liquidity became more evenly distributed. As the inflation rate remained 
more than 2 pps below the target of 5% from the second quarter of 2024 onward, the Central

by the Central Bank, and an estimate of the time frame within which the inflation target will be

While maintaining a flexible exchange rate policy, the Central Bank continued to rebuild gross 
official reserves through foreign exchange purchases. Considering the improved external 
sector conditions, the Central Bank also relaxed several capital flow management measures

sector conditions, the Central Bank also relaxed several capital flow management measures

In recent years, the Sri Lankan economy has 
faced more frequent and intense domestic and 
external shocks. Whilst some of these shocks 
have emanated from natural disasters, others 
were triggered by domestic and global man-
made actions. Heightened uncertainties caused 
by frequent and intense economic shocks affect 
consumption and savings decisions of households

consumption and savings decisions of households 
and production and investment decisions of 
businesses, hindering the growth potential of the 
country. Further, macro level decision making 
and policy formulation have become increasingly 
challenging due to these heightened uncertainties, 
since policy transmission channels weaken and 
policy responses become less predictable during 
economics crises.

policy responses become less predictable during

The socio-economic impacts of these shocks are 
multifaceted and can leave lasting scars on the 
economy. Generally, such shocks disproportionately 
burden vulnerable segments of the population, 
thereby exacerbating economic inequalities.
As uncertainty has become the ‘new normal’, 
future holds more challenges due to rapidly 
evolving technology, increased global conflicts, 
geopolitical fragmentation, climate change induced

geopolitical fragmentation, climate change induced 
natural disasters, transition into renewable energy, 
increased protectionism and various other shocks. 
Based on recent experiences during the pandemic 
and domestic economic crisis, these shocks can 
lead to significant macroeconomic instability, 
including setbacks in economic growth and 
episodes of high and volatile inflation, particularly 
when the economy lacks sufficient external and 
fiscal buffers and limited monetary policy space.

when the economy lacks sufficient external and

fiscal and external buffers are paramount to 
steer the economy through turbulent times. The 
importance of maintaining adequate buffers 
became evident during and in the aftermath

crisis preparedness and promoting risk sharing 
mechanisms, such as insurance, can help economic

crisis preparedness and promoting risk sharing 
mechanisms, such as insurance, can help economic

nets are also vital to cushion the adverse effects of 
economic shocks on vulnerable groups.

(c) The rate at which the Central Bank grants advances to banking institutions as the lender of last resort (LOLR). Up to April 2020, the Bank Rate was a fixed rate determined by the Monetary Board. Since 16 April 2020, the Bank Rate was allowed to be

determined automatically with a margin of 300 bps above the SLFR. Since 03 November 2022, Bank Rate was allowed to commensurately be adjusted in line with the monthly Average Weighted New Deposit Rate (AWNDR) published by the Central Bank 
with a margin of +700 bps. This margin was subsequently reduced to +300 bps with effect from 02 January 2023, with the resulting rate rounded to the nearest half percentage point. Since 01 March 2023, Bank Rate was delisted from monetary policy

instruments and it is to be considered as a policy instrument that the Central Bank uses as the LOLR to support the stability of the banking and financial system.

(f) The Average Weighted New Deposit Rate (AWNDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all new interest bearing rupee deposits mobilised by LCBs during a particular month.

(g) The Average Weighted New Fixed Deposit Rate (AWNFDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all new interest bearing rupee time deposits mobilised by LCBs during a particular month.

(e)  The rate at which the Central Bank grants advances to banking institutions as the lender of last resort. Up to April 2020, the Bank Rate was a fixed rate determined by the Monetary Board. Since

adjusted in line with the monthly Average Weighted New Deposit Rate (AWNDR) published by the Central Bank with a margin of +700 bps. This margin was subsequently reduced to +300 bps

with effect from 02 January 2023, with the resulting rate rounded to the nearest half percentage point. Since 01 March 2023, Bank Rate was delisted from monetary policy instruments and it 
is to be considered as a policy instrument that the Central Bank uses as the lender of last resort (LOLR) to support the stability of the banking and financial system.

arising out of commercial transactions, where there is no agreed rate of interest. The Governing Board of the Central Bank determines the Legal Rate and Market Rate for each year and 
publishes in the Government Gazette in the month of December to be applicable for the forthcoming year. The Legal Rate and the Market Rate for the year 2026 is 11.39% per annum.

Three years into the programme, it has delivered substantial  gains, moving the country from 
crisis to recovery and now towards stabilisation.  However,  the economy continues to face

struck just as recovery momentum was building, inflicting severe humanitarian and economic 
damage. Subsequently, in late February 2026, the Middle East conflict triggered a renewed

Sri Lanka's ability to navigate these sequential and compounding shocks—without abandoning

Sri Lanka's ability to navigate these sequential and compounding shocks—without abandoning

the infrastructure, agricultural lands, and irrigation systems. In response, emergency relief

responsibilities at all levels government.

Rule 2: Primary Balance Target
Section 14 of the PFMA requires that the MTFF include an annual primary balance target, defined

Section 14 of the PFMA requires that the MTFF include an annual primary balance target, defined 
as the difference between government revenue and primary expenditure (i.e., expenditure 
excluding interest payments), expressed as a percentage of forecast nominal GDP and set for 
the upcoming financial year and each of the four succeeding years. This target is required to 
be consistent with the debt reduction objective, linking the fiscal flow target to the stock-of-
debt anchor.

debt anchor.
This rule functions as the central medium-term fiscal anchor. Unlike a simple deficit rule, a 
primary balance rule focuses on the part of the fiscal position directly under government 
control (i.e., excluding the inherited cost of existing debt). A sustained primary surplus signals 
the Government's capacity to service debt over time. The IMF-EFF programme has established 
an overall primary balance target of +2.3 percent of GDP, and the PFMA institutionalises the

an overall primary balance target of +2.3 percent of GDP, and the PFMA institutionalises the 
practice of setting and publishing such targets in a rolling medium-term framework through 
the annual FSS.
Rule 3: Primary Expenditure Ceiling of 13% of GDP
Section 15 of the PFMA introduces an annual ceiling on primary expenditure—government 
spending excluding interest payments on public debt— which shall not exceed 13 percent

spending excluding interest payments on public debt— which shall not exceed 13 percent 
of estimated nominal GDP in each financial year. This ceiling is operationalised as an absolute 
rupee figure in the annual budget, derived from the GDP percentage limit.
The rule includes an escape clause that allows temporary deviation from the expenditure ceiling 
in the event of a natural disaster, epidemic, national security emergency, or a severe economic

in the event of a natural disaster, epidemic, national security emergency, or a severe economic 
downturn, subject to Parliamentary notification and the publication of a plan for returning to

Rule 4: Government Guarantee Ceiling of 7.5% of GDP
Section 17 of the PFMA caps the aggregate stock of outstanding government guarantees at 7.5

Section 17 of the PFMA caps the aggregate stock of outstanding government guarantees at 7.5 
percent of the average GDP of the relevant financial year and the two preceding financial years. 
This three-year average base reduces the ceiling's sensitivity to year-to-year GDP volatility, 
providing a more stable benchmark. The limit is subject to review every five years to ensure 
alignment with the prevailing debt reduction objective.

alignment with the prevailing debt reduction objective.
This rule directly addresses one of the key drivers of Sri Lanka's debt crisis: the accumulation 
of large contingent liabilities through guarantees extended to loss-making  SOEs, particularly 
CEB and CPC. By placing a statutory cap on the total guarantee stock, the PFMA limits the 
potential crystallization of off-balance-sheet liabilities into direct government debt.

Governance beyond the numbers
Well designed and credibly enforced fiscal rules are among the most powerful instruments 
of fiscal governance. The empirical literature finds a robust positive relationship between the 
presence of binding fiscal rules and lower public debt, smaller deficits, and stronger fiscal

presence of binding fiscal rules and lower public debt, smaller deficits, and stronger fiscal 
discipline, particularly in countries emerging from episodes of fiscal stress. The four rules 
introduced under the PFMA address governance not merely by imposing numerical limits, but 
by fundamentally changing how fiscal decisions are made, disclosed, and held to account. 
Each rule works through distinct governance channels.
Transparency: Making the Fiscal Position Visible and Verifiable

Transparency: Making the Fiscal Position Visible and Verifiable
A fundamental weakness of Sri Lanka's pre-crisis fiscal governance was opacity. Public debt 
had been systematically understated, SOE liabilities were kept off-balance sheet, and medium-
term fiscal plans were treated as non-binding. The PFMA's fiscal rules directly reverse this.
The debt reduction objective requires the Government to publicly disclose, in the annual

The debt reduction objective requires the Government to publicly disclose, in the annual 
FSS, a concrete timeframe and trajectory for reducing public debt to a sustainable level. The 
primary balance target reinforces this by requiring the Government to publish its projected 
fiscal path, expressed in standardized, comparable GDP terms, for five years forward. Citizens, 
market participants, and development partners are thereby enabled to assess not just the

market participants, and development partners are thereby enabled to assess not just the 
current fiscal position, but the Government's stated commitment and trajectory.
Most significantly for governance perspective, the government guarantee ceiling brings 
contingent liabilities—historically the least transparent segment of Sri Lanka's public finances— 
within a statutory disclosure and reporting framework. The PFMA requires the outstanding

within a statutory disclosure and reporting framework. The PFMA requires the outstanding 
stock of guarantees to be calculated, reported, and monitored against a binding limit at the 
end of every financial year. This converts what was previously an off-balance-sheet fiscal risk 
into a visible, auditable, and constrained liability. Fiscal transparency of this kind has been 
shown to be positively correlated with lower sovereign borrowing costs and stronger credit

shown to be positively correlated with lower sovereign borrowing costs and stronger credit 
ratings, as it reduces the information asymmetry between the government and its creditors.
Accountability: Creating Enforceable Commitments
Fiscal targets that exist only in budget speeches are easily abandoned. The FMRA's targets were 
amended multiple times without consequence, undermining any credibility the framework

amended multiple times without consequence, undermining any credibility the framework 
may have had. The PFMA's rules are structurally different; they are embedded in statute, and 
the Act requires a formal assessment of compliance or non-compliance with each target to 
be published in the FSS and in the final budget position report (Annual Report). Any deviation 
from the primary expenditure ceiling must be explained, and a plan for returning to compliance 
presented to Parliament.

presented to Parliament.
The primary balance target creates an explicitly measurable, annually assessed benchmark. 
Because the target is defined as a percentage of GDP and published five years ahead, it is both

The four fiscal rules introduced under the PFMA represent a meaningful advance in Sri Lanka's 
fiscal governance architecture. Rather than merely setting numerical limits, they provide 
Parliament and the public with a structured basis for  scrutinizing how fiscal decisions are made, 
disclosed, and held account. The debt reduction objective and primary balance target impose

Box 4.1 | Phasing out CESS: Transforming Sri Lanka’s Trade Landscape 
Sri Lanka is undertaking a major reform of its tariff structure through the phased removal of the 
CESS levy under the Export Development Act, No. 40 of 1979. This reform marks a decisive shift 
from a complex, protection-oriented regime toward a simpler, more transparent, and globally

from a complex, protection-oriented regime toward a simpler, more transparent, and globally 
competitive trade framework.
For years, CESS functioned as both a revenue source and a protective tool for domestic industries. 
However, its expansion—alongside other para-tariffs—has led to a fragmented tariff structure, 
increasing the cost of imported inputs and weakening export competitiveness. It has also reduced 
transparency and predictability in trade policy.

transparency and predictability in trade policy.
Recognizing these challenges, the Government has initiated a phased reform to rationalize tariffs, 
reduce production costs, and promote export-led growth.
Policy Framework and Implementation
The reform was introduced under Budget Proposal No. 34.6 of 2023 and implemented through 
Gazette No. 2325/06. It was further strengthened under Budget Proposal No. 35.3 of 2026, which

removed CESS on fabrics while introducing VAT to maintain competitive neutrality.
With Cabinet approval on 03 March 2026, Gazette No. 2479/38 formalized the phased removal 
of CESS on 2,634 HS codes over four years, aligned with commitments under the World Bank’s 
Development Policy Operation (DPO).

1. Overview
The introduction of the 4-Band Customs Import Duty (CID) framework, published on 03 March 
2026 under Gazette Notification No. 2478/03, with effect from 1 April 2026, marks a significant 
structural reform under Sri Lanka’s National Tariff Policy (NTP). The reform rationalizes the

structural reform under Sri Lanka’s National Tariff Policy (NTP). The reform rationalizes the 
existing tariff regime, enhances transparency, and aligns with international best practices.
The reform supports the national development agenda of “Thriving Nation, A Beautiful Country” 
and contributes towards achieving the medium-term export target.
2. Key Features of the Reform
The reform introduces a streamlined and standardized tariff structure with the following 
features:

The reform introduces a streamlined and standardized tariff structure with the following 
features:
• Adoption of a four-band tariff system
• Alignment with United Nations Broad Economic Categories (BEC) Rev.5
• Reduction of tariffs on inputs to support domestic production
• Rationalization of tariffs on consumption goods
• Maintenance of stability across the majority of tariff lines
3. Tariff Structure

• Maintenance of stability across the majority of tariff lines

03 March 2026, comprises a four-band Customs Import Duty (CID) structure consisting of 0

Key Tariff Adjustments under the 4-Band Structure
The following key adjustments have been introduced under the 4-Band CID Reform:
(a) Reduction of tariffs on intermediate goods 
Intermediate goods previously subject to 15 percent tariffs are reduced to 10 percent to 
lower input costs and enhance industrial competitiveness.

lower input costs and enhance industrial competitiveness.
(b) Rationalization of tariffs on consumption goods 
Consumption goods are restructured at 20 percent or 30 percent based on essentiality 
and domestic production considerations.
(c) Retention of selected goods at 20 percent 
Certain intermediate goods are temporarily retained at 20 percent, taking into account 
revenue implications and sector-specific considerations.
(d) Streamlining of mixed-rate structures

revenue implications and sector-specific considerations.
(d) Streamlining of mixed-rate structures 
Mixed-rate tariffs are rationalized and adjusted in line with the revised tariff bands.
(e) Maintenance of stability across tariff lines 
A majority of tariff lines remain unchanged to ensure continuity and investor confidence.
(f) Sector-specific adjustments 
Targeted adjustments are made in selected sectors to balance production support, 
revenue mobilization, and consumer considerations.

revenue mobilization, and consumer considerations.
(g) Exclusions from the 4-band structure 
Goods subject to Specific rates, as well as tobacco and liquor products, remain outside 
the framework to maintain revenue certainty and policy objectives.

The 4-Band Tariff Reform establishes a streamlined, transparent, and rules-based tariff 
framework aligned with international best practices in goods classification and national 
economic objectives. Lower tariffs on intermediate and capital goods, together with the 
application of 20 percent or 30 percent bands on consumption goods, support industrial

application of 20 percent or 30 percent bands on consumption goods, support industrial

Cyclone Ditwah, which made landfall in Sri Lanka on 28 November 2025, caused extensive 
damage across 22 districts, severely affecting lives, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure. 
The disaster led to widespread displacement, disruption of essential services, and significant 
impacts on economic activity. Notwithstanding these challenges, the resilience demonstrated

impacts on economic activity. Notwithstanding these challenges, the resilience demonstrated 
by affected communities, local authorities, and emergency responders has been commendable.
In response, the Government of Sri Lanka, under the mandate of the “Rebuilding Sri Lanka” 
Presidential Task Force, initiated a comprehensive Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA). 
The assessment was led by the Disaster Management Centre and the Ministry of Defense,

The assessment was led by the Disaster Management Centre and the Ministry of Defense, 
in collaboration with the Department of National Planning of the Ministry of Finance, with 
the support of all relevant government agencies and key development partners. The PDNA 
provides a rigorous, evidence-based evaluation of damages, economic losses, and recovery 
needs, forming the basis for coordinated recovery planning and resource mobilization.

economy now accounts for approximately 15 percent of global GDP—roughly $16 trillion—

economy now accounts for approximately 15 percent of global GDP—roughly $16 trillion—
and is fundamentally reshaping how nations produce, trade, and grow. Forecasts indicate it 
will expand at a compound annual growth rate of 7 percent, reaching $16.5 trillion by 2028 
and representing 17 percent of global GDP 1. For a small island nation like Sri Lanka—still in 
the process of rebuilding from its most severe post-independence crisis—this is not merely a

the process of rebuilding from its most severe post-independence crisis—this is not merely a 
global trend to observe, but a critical opportunity to seize.
The digital economy extends far beyond smartphones and social media. It encompasses 
e-commerce, digital finance, cloud computing, IT-enabled services, artificial intelligence, and 
the data infrastructure that underpins modern governance and industry. Research shows that

the data infrastructure that underpins modern governance and industry. Research shows that 
every dollar invested in digital transformation generates $8.30 in returns within a country’s 
broader digital economy—a multiplier effect few other investment categories can match 2. 
Countries that lead in digital infrastructure advance decisively, while those that fall behind risk 
permanent exclusion from the fastest-growing segment of global trade.

permanent exclusion from the fastest-growing segment of global trade.
Sri Lanka’s economic recovery, which rebounded with approximately 5 percent growth in 
2024 following a sharp contraction, has demonstrated resilience. However, the country must 
now shift from stabilization to transformation. The digital economy offers a clear pathway to 
achieve this.

Box 5.3 l  Social Safety Nets
Sri Lanka has a long history of social protection systems, which began with traditional 
community support mechanisms and gradually evolved into formal, government-sponsored 
welfare programs. During the British colonial period, limited forms of government assistance 
such as poor relief and pensions were introduced; however, these were not implemented on a

such as poor relief and pensions were introduced; however, these were not implemented on a 
large scale. Following independence in 1948, Sri Lanka developed into a strong welfare state, 
introducing policies such as free education, free healthcare, and food subsidies etc. However, 
with the introduction of the open economic policy in 1977, there was a gradual shift from 
universal welfare benefits toward targeted assistance programs. Accordingly, programs such

universal welfare benefits toward targeted assistance programs. Accordingly, programs such 
as Janasaviya and Samurdhi, which included financial assistance and community development 
initiatives aimed at poverty alleviation, were introduced.
In particular, during the period from 2020 to 2022, in response to the COVID-19 global pandemic 
and the most severe economic crisis faced by Sri Lanka, efforts were made to strengthen and

and the most severe economic crisis faced by Sri Lanka, efforts were made to strengthen and 
improve the efficiency of the social protection system to ensure better support for vulnerable 
populations without exclusion. By 2023, the Government restructured its welfare system and 
introduced the Aswesuma program to expand coverage, improve efficiency, and enhance 
targeting accuracy. Beneficiaries are selected based on a multidimensional poverty index.

targeting accuracy. Beneficiaries are selected based on a multidimensional poverty index. 
To address shortcomings in previous programs and improve beneficiary coverage while 
minimizing inclusion and exclusion errors, a Social Registry Information System (SRIS) containing 
information on social protection beneficiaries has been established. Through the Aswesuma 
program, monthly financial assistance is provided to low-income households categorized as 
extremely poor, poor, and vulnerable.

extremely poor, poor, and vulnerable.
In addition, the annual budget allocation for this program has been increased, along with 
the number of beneficiaries. Accordingly, effective from January 2025, the allowance for the 
extremely poor category has been increased from Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 17,500, while the allowance 
for the poor category has been increased from Rs. 8,500 to Rs. 10,000. The allowance of Rs. 
5,000 for the vulnerable category continues to be provided without interruption.

5,000 for the vulnerable category continues to be provided without interruption.
Furthermore, the program has been expanded to include support for elderly individuals, 
persons with disabilities, and individuals suffering from chronic kidney disease within low-
income families. From April 2025, the monthly allowance for kidney patients and persons with

aimed at strengthening fiscal transparency and public accountability. It requires the preparation 
and publication of a public-friendly version of the annual budget, designed to communicate the 
key elements of government fiscal policy in a clear, concise, and easily understandable manner.

key elements of government fiscal policy in a clear, concise, and easily understandable manner.

Departments, and expenditure Heads—can be highly technical and difficult for the general public 
to interpret. As a result, many citizens and taxpayers may not fully understand how public funds are 
raised and utilized.

strengthen the country’s public debt management framework with the objective of restoring debt

strengthen the country’s public debt management framework with the objective of restoring debt 
sustainability, improving fiscal resilience, and enhancing macroeconomic stability. A major milestone 
in this reform journey was the enactment of the Public Debt Management Act, No. 33 of 2024 (PDMA), 
which established a unified legal and institutional framework for public debt management through 
the establishment of the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO). By consolidating debt management

the establishment of the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO). By consolidating debt management 
functions that were previously dispersed across multiple institutions, the new framework significantly 
strengthened coordination, governance, accountability, and operational efficiency in public debt 
management.

During 2025, several important measures were introduced to further strengthen the legal and 
institutional framework governing public debt management. The issuance of Public Debt Management 
Regulations No. 01/2025 and No. 02/2025, together with operational guidelines and institutional 
procedures, significantly enhanced governance arrangements, risk management practices, and internal 
controls within the debt management process. These reforms paved the way for a more rules-based,

controls within the debt management process. These reforms paved the way for a more rules-based, 
transparent, and disciplined approach to debt management. In order to further strengthen institutional 
coordination and governance, the Public Debt Coordination Committee (PDCC) was appointed in 
January 2025 to facilitate effective coordination between debt management, fiscal policy, and monetary 
policy operations.

A key reform achievement was the introduction and publication of Sri Lanka’s first Medium-Term Debt 
Management Strategy (MTDS) for the period 2025– 2029 and Annual Borrowing Plan (ABP) for the year 
2025 under the PDMA. This marked a paradigm shift from ad-hoc borrowing practices towards a more 
strategic and cost-risk based approach to government financing, ensuring greater consistency with the 
Government’s medium-term fiscal and macroeconomic objectives.

Box 6.1 l  Strengthening Sri Lanka’s Public Debt Management Framework: Paving the Way for a

Another landmark reform was the transfer of responsibility for conducting domestic government 
securities auctions from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka to the PDMO in December 2025. This transition

strengthened the institutional separation between debt management and monetary policy functions 
in line with international best practices, while enhancing the operational independence and 
governance of government borrowing activities.
To support this transition, the Debt and Cash Management Committee (DCMC) and the Auction Steering 
Committee (ASC) were established within the Ministry of Finance to oversee strategic borrowing

Committee (ASC) were established within the Ministry of Finance to oversee strategic borrowing 
decisions and government securities auction operations. These institutional arrangements further 
strengthened governance, transparency, and decision-making within the domestic borrowing process.
The reform framework also introduced stronger mechanisms for managing fiscal risks associated with 
government guarantees and on-lending operations through the adoption of risk-based measures such as

guarantee fees and on-lending premiums, thereby improving the management of contingent liabilities 
and safeguarding public finances.
Enhancing transparency and investor engagement has been another important pillar of Sri Lanka’s 
public debt management reforms. Measures have been introduced to improve the availability, quality, 
and timeliness of debt-related information, while strengthening communication and engagement with

and timeliness of debt-related information, while strengthening communication and engagement with 
investors and other stakeholders. These initiatives have contributed to improving investor confidence 
and reinforcing Sri Lanka’s commitment to transparent and accountable public financial management 
practices.
Overall, Sri Lanka’s public debt management reforms signify a major transformation in the country’s

debt management architecture, laying a strong foundation for prudent borrowing, improved fiscal risk 
management, and long-term debt sustainability.

(Government Agencies (Ministries, Departments, District Secretariats, Special Spending Units, Foreign 
Missions), Public Enterprises and Provincial Councils & Local Governments) and to formulate and implement

Non - Financial Assets management policies, identifying idle resources and ensuring effective use of these 
assets, to strengthen the development framework of the Government.

the Public Assets Management Law.

recording system is established, which consists of essential information including assets valuation required

for the Non-Financial Assets management. The design, software development, implementation, improvement

06. Nature and Purpose of Reserves 
 The Government creates and maintains 
reserves in terms of specific local 
requirements.
07.  Consolidated Fund 
 The funds of the Republic not allocated 
by law to specific purposes form the 
Consolidated Fund into which shall be 
paid the produce of all taxes, levies, rates 
and duties and all other revenues and

paid the produce of all taxes, levies, rates 
and duties and all other revenues and 
receipts of the Republic not allocated to 
specific purposes.
08.  Contingency Fund
 A Fund Created by Parliament by law for 
the purpose of providing for urgent and 
unforeseen expenditure.
09.  General Fund 
 The balance of the General Fund 
represents the cumulative financial 
performance of the Government after 
accounting for all receipts and payments 
through the Consolidated Fund and

accounting for all receipts and payments 
through the Consolidated Fund and 
the adjustments recorded in Nominal 
Accounts. Surpluses or deficits arising 
during the reporting period are reflected 
directly in the General Fund balance.
10.  Foreign Loan Adjustment Accounts
 Accounts created for recording loan 
receipts and reimbursements for 
expenditure incurred.
